summary.text: A pull quote stating that small, timely investments through the fund can save lives and cut the costs of responding to outbreaks and emergencies.

sections.extract: The CFE has proved that a small investment at the right time can pay life-saving dividends and dramatically reduce the direct costs of controlling outbreaks and responding to emergencies.

sections.title: Key figures in 2020

summary.text: Explains that the Contingency Fund for Emergencies was set up in 2015 to let WHO deploy resources quickly before other funding mechanisms such as CERF are available, releasing funds within 24 hours. It notes that releases cover response activities, staff and supplies and are subject to WHO financial rules and annual reporting.

sections.extract: was established in 2015 as a key component of the reforms undertaken by WHO to strengthen its role in emergencies. The unique benefit of the CFE is that it can be used to rapidly deploy WHO and global health emergency workforce assets for control and containment of a disease outbreak or to strengthen the health response in humanitarian crises before other funding mechanisms can be triggered. sections.title: CFE in health emergencies

summary.text: Reports that in 2020 the fund supported responses to 14 emergencies in 13 countries plus COVID-19, releasing nearly US$ 44 million, with about 80% going to COVID-19 and to two Ebola outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

sections.extract: The CFE enabled WHO to mount rapid and sustained responses to 14 separate emergencies in 13 countries and one global response (COVID-19) in 2020. A total of nearly US$ 44 million was released in 2020. Table 1 contains a list of all approved releases by event in 2020. Some 80% of funding released from the CFE went to support just three events in 2020: the two Ebola outbreaks in the Democratic Republic of the Congo

sections.title: Expenditures

summary.text: Details 2020 fund expenditures, including bridging funding gaps in the protracted North Kivu Ebola response, US$ 5.3 million for the Equateur Ebola outbreak and US$ 12.9 million for early COVID-19 response. It lists other emergencies supported, reports that most small allocations were released within 24 hours, and gives a table of releases by event and a chart of refund rates by year.

sections.extract: last year. In 2020, the CFE continued to support critical, life-saving operations in response to the Ebola outbreak in North Kivu, DRC, which started in 2018. sections.title: Replenishing the CFE

summary.text: Explains that the fund was designed to be revolving but has been hard to replenish, with about 40% of 2020 allocations refunded. It notes that refunds vary by emergency, with most COVID-19 releases reimbursed but Ebola releases less so, and presents a table of releases and refunds by event.

sections.extract: The CFE was conceived by Member States and launched in 2015 as a revolving fund. Costs initially incurred against CFE allocations would be reimbursed by donor funding to the WHO emergency response at country level and unspent funds would be returned. sections.title: CFE contributions

summary.text: Reports that 13 Member States contributed nearly US$ 23 million in 2020, down from previous years likely because of the focus on funding COVID-19, with Austria joining for the first time. Tables and a chart show contributions by country and for 2015–2020, and the block notes how the fund enabled rapid responses amid multiple crises.

sections.extract: In 2020, 13 Member States generously made contributions to the CFE totaling almost US$ 23 million (Table 3). Austria joined the list of contributors for the first time. Contributions dropped from the previous two years. This was likely to be as a result of the exceptional focus last year on addressing and fully funding the COVID-19 response (Figure 3). See Annex 3 for a complete list of CFE contributors since 2015.

sections.title: ENABLING A SWIFT RESPONSE

summary.text: Gives examples of rapid responses enabled by the fund, including over US$ 2 million released within 24 hours after the Beirut port explosion, support for the Equateur Ebola response, airlifted supplies in Syria, and cyclone response in Vanuatu. It notes support for COVID-19 supply chains and argues that small, early releases had outsized impact. The block also describes WHO's work in Lebanon on medicines, dialysis supplies and a mental health hotline.

sections.extract: For example, more than US$ 2 million was released within 24 hours through the CFE to respond to the urgent humanitarian health needs following the Beirut port explosions. sections.title: Life-saving health response to Tropical Cyclone Harold in Vanuatu

summary.text: Describes WHO support in Vanuatu after Cyclone Harold despite COVID-19 restrictions, including emergency medical team deployment, surveillance tools and repairs to three health facilities, later reimbursed by CERF. It then outlines the health crisis in north-eastern Syria after displacement in 2019, where few health centres were fully functional and WHO used the fund to airlift supplies when borders closed.

sections.extract: ©WHO / Philippe Metois CFE funds supported Vanuatu Ministry of Health activities in response to Tropical Cyclone Harold. WHO Vanuatu provided critical rapid response support, despite COVID-19 restrictions which led to delays in the arrival of key resources and a lack of military logistical support. sections.title: Overcoming closed borders to provide life-saving emergency supplies to north-eastern Syria

summary.text: Shows how fund support helped deliver supplies to partners in north-eastern Syria, then introduces the 11th Ebola outbreak in Equateur Province, Democratic Republic of the Congo, which ended in November 2020 with 119 confirmed cases and 55 deaths. It notes the added strain of COVID-19 and the decentralised, community-based response.

sections.title: Defeating the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s 11th Ebola outbreak while fighting the COVID-19 pandemic

summary.text: Tells the story of community resistance to Ebola in Mbandaka, where youth leaders persuaded people to accept treatment and vaccination, and describes ultra-cold freezers used to vaccinate in areas without electricity. It credits the fund with launching and sustaining the response and calls for continued vigilance. The block ends with the start of the COVID-19 supply chain section, describing pandemic supply networks supported by early fund releases.

sections.title: Rapid scale-up of the COVID-19 Supply Chain System to provide timely and equitable access to critical health supplies

summary.text: Describes how early Contingency Fund for Emergencies releases helped WHO build the COVID-19 supply chain system, including national planning support, supply catalogues, demand management, pooled procurement and stockpiling, and logistics through the World Food Programme. It presents this pooled, equitable approach as a lasting shift in pandemic preparedness and calls for sustainable financing of WHO, with the fund as a key part of emergency response.

sections.extract: and equitable access to critical health supplies ©WHO / Blink Media – Natalie Naccache CFE funds facilitated distribution of critical health supplies.
